title: Online Election
statement:
An election is recorded as two arrays of equal length: vote `i` went to candidate `persons[i]` and happened at time `times[i]`. Build a class `TopVotedCandidate` that answers "who was ahead at time `t`?".

- `TopVotedCandidate(persons, times)` stores the election.
- `q(t)` returns the candidate leading once every vote with time at most `t` has been counted (a vote cast exactly at `t` is included). The leader is the candidate with the most counted votes; if several candidates share that count, the leader is the one among them whose latest vote is the most recent.

`times` is strictly increasing, and every query satisfies `t >= times[0]`, so at least one vote is always counted.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls are made to q
notes:
## Intuition

The leader only changes when a vote arrives, so there are just `n` possible answers: the leader right after each vote. Recounting all votes for every query works but costs O(n) per query. Instead, replay the votes once in the constructor and remember the leader after each one. A query then needs the last vote at or before `t`, and because `times` is sorted, binary search finds it in O(log n).

## Approach

1. In the constructor keep `times`, a vote tally `counts`, and the running `leader`.
2. For each vote, add one to `counts[person]`. If `person` now has at least as many votes as `leader`, `person` becomes the leader: they either lead outright or tie with the most recent vote.
3. Push the current `leader` onto `leaders`, so `leaders[i]` is the leader just after vote `i`.
4. `q(t)`: binary search for the largest index `left` with `times[left] <= t`, using an upper middle `mid` so the range always shrinks.
5. Return `leaders[left]`.

## Example 1, step by step

Votes `[0,1,1,0,0,1,0]` at `[0,5,10,15,20,25,30]`. Replaying: after vote 0 leader 0; vote 1 ties 1–1, so 1 leads; vote 2 gives 1 two votes; vote 3 ties 2–2, so 0 leads; vote 4 puts 0 ahead; vote 5 ties 3–3, so 1; vote 6 gives 0. So `leaders = [0,1,1,0,0,1,0]`. `q(3)` finds index 0 → `0`; `q(12)` index 2 → `1`; `q(25)` index 5 → `1`; `q(15)` index 3 → `0`; `q(24)` index 4 → `0`; `q(8)` index 1 → `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) to build, O(log n) per query.
- Space: O(n) for `counts` and `leaders`.

## Pitfalls

- Use `>=`, not `>`, when comparing with the leader's count: a tie goes to the candidate who just voted.
- The search wants the last time `<= t`, not the first time `>= t`; a vote exactly at `t` counts.
- With `left = mid` in the loop, `mid` must round up or the loop never ends when two indices remain.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `times` | the sorted vote times |
| `leaders` | `leaders[i]` is the leader just after vote `i` |
| `counts` | votes received so far by each candidate |
| `leader`, `person` | the current leader and the candidate of the vote being replayed |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary-search bounds over vote indices |
